records.title: Digital Twin CAD Assembly Model
records.reflection:
I designed and assembled a full CAD model of Shadow’s physical hardware in Fusion 360 — the base frame, all 4 motors with their feet and lock nuts, the Navio2 flight controller mounted on its standoffs, the companion computer, and the LiDAR mast with its deck and pucks, plus all 4 propellers (2 CW, 2 CCW). This wasn’t a rough concept — I modeled each part and assembled them together the way they’ll actually sit on the real drone.

The purpose was twofold. First, to replace the placeholder box/cylinder geometry my Gazebo simulation had been using — functionally correct for physics, but not a real representation of the drone I’m actually designing. This CAD assembly is what makes my digital twin an actual twin: a 3D model that matches my real hardware, not a stand-in. Second, it’s the foundation for the exploded/X-ray component-inspection view I’ve scoped out for the dashboard — click into any part, see its specs, per drone model. That feature can’t happen without this asset existing first.

I exported the assembly via fusion2urdf into the mesh files my sim now uses, so this is the real engineering deliverable, not just prep work — the integration debugging that came after (getting the meshes positioned correctly in Gazebo, fixing mislabelled propellers, decimating the heaviest meshes for render performance) was a separate downstream task of making my model work inside the simulator, not part of the CAD design work itself.
